analysis.one_liner: Guaranteed health coverage for every American through regulated insurance pools with capped premiums and out-of-pocket costs.
analysis.headline: The Senate's version of the Clinton health plan, guaranteeing coverage to every American, was introduced with 30 Senate cosponsors in November 1993, heard once in committee in April 1994, and never received a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Health Security Act would have guaranteed a comprehensive health benefit package to every legal resident, with annual out-of-pocket costs capped at $1,500 per person and $3,000 per family. It would have barred insurers from denying coverage for preexisting conditions or canceling coverage, required employers to help pay premiums, and capped the growth of premiums. It also added a Medicare prescription drug benefit with manufacturer rebates and funded home- and community-based long-term care for people with disabilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Every legal resident would have gained guaranteed coverage they could not lose by changing jobs or getting sick, with no denial for preexisting conditions and out-of-pocket costs capped at $1,500 per person or $3,000 per family. Low-income families would have gotten premium discounts and reduced cost sharing. Seniors would have gained a Medicare prescription drug benefit with manufacturer rebates, and people with disabilities would have gained home- and community-based long-term care services. People in states that chose to do so could have opted into a single-payer system.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone needing health coverage, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Entitles every legal resident to a comprehensive benefit package covering hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health services, preventive care, dental and vision care, and more, issued through a health security card

Caps annual out-of-pocket costs at $1,500 per individual and $3,000 per family, and requires plans to accept all applicants without excluding preexisting conditions, imposing waiting periods, or canceling coverage
Requires employers to make premium payments and gives low-income families premium discounts and reduced cost sharing, with federal payments covering cash-assistance recipients
Adds a Medicare outpatient prescription drug benefit with manufacturer rebates and directs an advisory council to review the launch prices of new breakthrough drugs
Caps the growth of health premiums through a National Health Board-administered premium target system, and requires competitive premium bids from plans
Establishes home- and community-based long-term care services for people with disabilities and strengthens standards for long-term care insurance to protect consumers
Repeals the insurance industry's antitrust exemption for health benefits under the McCarran-Ferguson Act and cracks down on health care fraud with new criminal penalties
Lets any state, with federal approval, opt into a statewide single-payer system

analysis.who_pays: Employers would have owed premium payments for their workers, with rates varying by firm size and average wages, plus assessments on corporate alliance employers and companies with retiree health costs. Smokers would have paid higher federal excise taxes on cigarettes and other tobacco products. Shareholders of S corporations and certain limited partners would have owed more self-employment tax. Federal and state governments would have financed coverage for cash-assistance recipients and new public health programs, and Medicare payment updates to hospitals would have been reduced to help pay for the plan.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, smokers, taxpayers, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The mandate cuts both ways: every eligible individual would have been required to enroll in a health plan and pay any required premium, so people who preferred to go uninsured would have been forced to buy coverage

The bill would have created a National Health Board of seven presidential appointees with sweeping power to define benefits, set premium targets, and regulate plans, concentrating enormous economic authority in a new federal body
Costs landed on identifiable groups: employers faced new premium obligations and assessments, cigarette taxes rose, and Medicare hospital payment updates were cut to help finance coverage
The comprehensive package still excluded services many people consider essential, including hearing aids, adult eyeglasses and contacts, in vitro fertilization, and most orthodontic work
Mental health and substance abuse coverage carried strict limits before 2001, including an annual cap of 30 inpatient or residential days and 30 outpatient psychotherapy visits

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains for ordinary people were enormous on paper: universal guaranteed coverage, protection against losing insurance when sick or between jobs, and hard caps on out-of-pocket costs. The costs were real but broadly diffused — employer mandates, higher tobacco taxes, and Medicare payment cuts — while the design kept private insurers in business as regulated contractors rather than replacing them, a compromise that spread the cost across employers, consumers, and government. The main honest criticism, beyond the new federal board's power, is that the plan's complexity (alliances, premium caps, corporate and regional tracks, transition rules) would have been difficult to administer, and its cost-control mechanism relied on untested federal premium targets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat on the Senate calendar while the Finance Committee held a single round of hearings; it was never voted out of committee and never came to a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senate Majority Leader George Mitchell introduced the Health Security Act on November 20, 1993 on behalf of himself and 29 other senators, 29 of them Democrats and one, Jim Jeffords, a Republican; it was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders
The Senate Finance Committee held hearings on provisions of the bill on April 26, 1994 — the only committee action of any kind in the bill's history
No committee markup, no floor debate, and no vote ever followed; the bill remained on the calendar until the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995
The narrower insurance portability reforms that eventually passed instead were enacted in 1996 as HIPAA, in the following Congress

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, employers who would have owed new premium payments, and drug makers were better off because the bill died — they avoided premium caps, guaranteed enrollment, a Medicare drug rebate requirement, and the loss of their antitrust exemption. The millions of Americans the bill would have covered gained nothing from its failure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, large employers, and drug makers

for.name: George J. Mitchell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on behalf of 30 senators and had it placed on the Senate calendar; his name is on the bill as sponsor

for.name: Senate cosponsors
for.role: 30 senators — 29 Democrats and 1 Republican (Jim Jeffords) — including Ted Kennedy, Pat Moynihan, Tom Daschle, and Jay Rockefeller

for.name: Daniel Patrick Moynihan
for.what_they_did: His committee held the only hearings on the bill, on April 26, 1994

against.name: George J. Mitchell
against.what_they_did: Announced in August 1994 that the health care bill would not be brought to the Senate floor, effectively declaring it dead for the year

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Industry coalition, including the Health Insurance Association of America's 'Harry and Louise' advertising campaign
against.what_they_did: Ran a national advertising and lobbying campaign against the plan's mandates and regulated alliances

against.name: Bob Dole
against.what_they_did: Led Senate Republican opposition to the Clinton health plan and offered alternative proposals

sides.party_line_note: All 29 Democratic cosponsors came from the Democratic caucus, with Jim Jeffords the sole Republican cosponsor; no roll-call vote ever occurred to test the split.

industries.note: The bill would have replaced much of the individual and small-group insurance market with state-run 'alliances' where plans compete under premium caps, guaranteed enrollment, and community rating — and it repealed the industry's antitrust exemption for health benefits. The industry's core underwriting practices would have been outlawed, which is why insurers fought it hardest.

industries.industry: Employers, especially large and mid-sized firms
industries.note: Employers would have been required to make premium payments for their workers, with rates scaled to firm size and wages, plus assessments on corporate alliance employers and firms with retiree health obligations. Small employers were among the loudest opponents of the mandate.

The bill created a Medicare outpatient drug benefit and required manufacturer rebates, and set up an advisory council to review whether launch prices of new breakthrough drugs were reasonable — a direct check on drug pricing.
Higher federal excise taxes on cigarettes and other tobacco products helped finance the coverage expansion, directly costing the industry sales.

Teaching hospitals would have gained dedicated payments funded through the alliance system, and low-income hospitals would have received assistance payments, but Medicare payment updates for inpatient services were cut to help finance the bill.

Certified health plans, including HMOs, would have gained access to millions of guaranteed enrollees through the alliances with premiums largely paid by employers and government, but under strict premium caps, community rating, and quality regulation.
